title: Two Years of Rule: Achievement or Agony?
translatorNote: This translation is intended to carry Kalaignar's voice into clear, contemporary English rather than recast the letter as literary or academic prose. It preserves the source's argument, political directness, rhetorical questions, repetition, irony, factual detail, and paragraph order. Names, dates, figures, quotations, and intentional English expressions are retained. Where Tamil idiom cannot be reproduced literally without sounding unnatural, the English follows its sense and rhetorical force without adding claims absent from the source. The original Tamil is reproduced in full below the translation and remains the authoritative text. `Udanpirappē` is retained in Tamil transliteration rather than flattened into “brother,” “sister,” or “comrade.” Literally evoking “one born alongside me,” Kalaignar uses it as a distinctive address of shared identity, equality, affection, and solidarity within the movement. Letter-specific notes: 1. The source's figures for the free-land distribution scheme are translated exactly as printed and are not independently recalculated or reconciled. 2. `நிதி நிலைக் குழு` is rendered **Standing Finance Committee**, following the source's own English parenthesis. 3. `உறுதிமொழிக் குழு` is rendered **Assurance Committee**, preserving the source institutional term. 4. The letter's allegations about crimes, advertising, defamation cases and government conduct are presented as Kalaignar's claims and argument, not independently verified assertions. 5. The source's contrast between Rules 110 and 111 is preserved as printed.
paragraphs: The 2013–2014 Budget session concluded on 16 May 2013. The Assembly was kept in session until the very day on which the AIADMK government completed two years in office. On the final day, after the leaders of parties very close to the ruling party had praised Chief Minister Jayalalithaa to the skies, she thanked them and read out the long speech she had already prepared. A large part of that lengthy reply was spent offering explanations for the various issues I had raised—and even those explanations were delivered in the “civilised” style that is uniquely hers.

During these two years in office, she has read more than a hundred announcements in the Assembly under Rule 110. Those statements concern departments that are under the responsibility of various ministers. I had asked: why did she not allow the ministers concerned to read them, instead of the Chief Minister herself reading every one of them day after day? What, then, are all those ministers there for? In reply, the Chief Minister said that during debates on demands for grants, after members raise requests, she consults officials and then makes the announcements herself.

But after members have expressed their views and officials have been consulted, could not the ministers of the departments concerned themselves have read those announcements under Rule 110? Could at least some of those more than hundred announcements not have been read through the respective ministers? Or has Rule 110 now been changed into something that only the Chief Minister is qualified to read—a special privilege belonging to the Chief Minister alone? On this, the Chief Minister said nothing in her long reply.

Nor is that all. The Chief Minister said in her reply that after members raised requests during the demands-for-grants debates, she consulted officials and then read announcements under Rule 110. But the officials who prepared the reply seem to have forgotten that many of the announcements she read were based on no request raised by any Assembly member.

For example, there were announcements that a paperboard factory would be established in Tiruchirappalli district with an investment of ₹1,200 crore; that an Ennore deep-sea port and a floating liquefied natural-gas terminal in Nagapattinam district would be implemented with an investment of ₹3,500 crore; and that a multi-storey industrial complex would be established at Thirumazhisai. There were no reports that any member had raised these as demands in the Assembly.

While speaking in thanks in the Assembly, the Chief Minister gave a long list of schemes that the AIADMK government had announced and brought into implementation during these two years. But every one of the schemes she read out in the Assembly had already appeared that very morning, on the 16th, in all the English and Tamil newspapers—in the form of four-page government advertisements in each newspaper. Except for Murasoli and Dinakaran, those four-page advertisements appeared in all newspapers, including Theekkathir.

It would help the public to know how many crores of rupees of taxpayers' money the AIADMK government spent on those advertisements and how much was spent on advertising during these two years of AIADMK rule. My point is not that governments should not advertise. Advertisements were issued during DMK rule too. But there must be some measure and some limit.

When public money is poured out on newspapers in such excessive quantities in the name of advertising, it can indirectly become an inducement not to publish news critical of the government in a democratic manner consistent with journalistic principles. If newspapers that write against the government do not receive advertisements worth crores of rupees, then when forced to choose between crores and the newspaper itself, which newspaper will be able to write impartially about the government's shortcomings and perform its duty?

I had asked: what is the financial source for the schemes announced by the Chief Minister under Rule 110? Will the money come from the allocations already made in the Budget? Will funds be allotted separately? Or are these merely “announcements”? Why were so many announcements not made in the Budget itself? Why did departmental ministers not make them while replying to demands for grants? To this, she argued: “Does someone who has been Chief Minister five times and Finance Minister four times not know the procedures for making financial allocations?”

I asked those questions precisely because I know those procedures to some extent. Has there ever been any previous government in which the Chief Minister herself read out so many announcements in the Assembly and was followed every day by speeches of praise?

In reply to my question, the Chief Minister said: “For new schemes announced after the Budget is presented, when the full financial size of the scheme has not yet been defined, it is not possible to make an allocation in the Budget. Therefore, separate Government Orders are issued for new schemes without allocations; they are treated as ‘new works’ and ‘new sub-works’, and the required funds are fully allotted in the Revised Estimates.”

I accept this completely. That is the truth. But only a certain amount of funding can be sought through Revised Estimates. If announcements are made on a scale greater than what ought to have been stated in the Budget itself, and all of them are then to be funded through Revised Estimates, the amount required will be very large. How is that money to be raised?

That is why, before the Budget is presented, meetings of the Standing Finance Committee take place over several days. Each minister discusses, with senior officials of the department, which schemes should be included in the Budget and which schemes should be announced in the reply. The Chief Secretary and Finance Secretary also participate, and the Chief Minister decides which schemes may be included. Those schemes then find a place in the Budget.

Instead of that process, what kind of procedure is it for the Chief Minister suddenly to decide on ordinary announcements worth even ₹1 crore or ₹2 crore relating to individual departments, come to the House and read them herself rather than allowing the departmental minister to do so—and then for the minister of that department to rise, like the opposition members, as though hearing the announcement for the first time, praise the Chief Minister, and for the Chief Minister to delight in hearing it?

It is not right for Jayalalithaa to imagine herself a Rajaji and try to divert the truth by narrating a little story of Ramakrishna Paramahamsa. In her reply she cited only one example: “Making mere announcements is an art mastered by Mr Karunanidhi. In 2006 he said that at least two acres of land would be given to every poor landless agricultural family. Until the end, land was not given to poor landless agricultural families.” Poor thing—perhaps that one example was all she could find! But is even that example true?

As promised in the DMK's 2006 election manifesto, the scheme to distribute land free of cost to poor landless agricultural labourers and farmers was launched in Tiruvallur district on 17 September 2006. Under this scheme, up to 15 February 2011, 45,064.62 acres were given to 41,970 Adi Dravidars; 3,872.46 acres to 3,277 Scheduled Tribes; 82,222.69 acres to 66,790 Backward Class beneficiaries; 62,084.18 acres to 58,269 Most Backward Class beneficiaries; and 19,750.65 acres to 8,692 people from other classes. In all, during DMK rule, 212,995 acres of developed land were distributed free to 179,002 families of poor landless agricultural labourers and farmers. Chief Minister Jayalalithaa can obtain the records still available in the department and verify this. If she wants the details of the dates and districts in which land-distribution functions were held during DMK rule, I am ready to provide them in full.
And those functions were not conducted through “video conferencing”. I personally went and distributed the land. Even reading the newspapers of those days would establish that.

Therefore, making empty announcements is not an art I mastered. The DMK is a movement accustomed to doing what it says and saying what it does. Indeed, if officials with a conscience are asked, they can explain that I have even been accustomed to doing, in the interests of the State, things I had not previously announced.

The Chief Minister who questions me—did she or did she not announce in the AIADMK election manifesto that sugarcane farmers would be paid ₹2,500 per tonne? Now that she has completed two years in office and issued four-page advertisements, why did those advertisements say nothing about the sugarcane price?

The Chief Minister sarcastically asked whether someone who had been Chief Minister five times did not know this. I had asked how she read under Rule 110 an explanatory statement that ought to have been read under Rule 111. I will not childishly ask whether someone who has been Chief Minister three times does not know even this.

The Chief Minister also cited a few examples in the Assembly to show which of the more than hundred statements she had read under Rule 110 had actually been implemented. Once the Chief Minister or ministers announce something in the Assembly, it must be implemented; otherwise the Assurance Committee, made up of Assembly members, will raise questions. But what happened to the following schemes announced by the Chief Minister under Rule 110?
On 8 September 2011—about a year and a half earlier—she announced a satellite town at Thirumazhisai at an estimated cost of ₹2,160 crore, with 12,000 multi-storey housing units.
On 3 May 2012 she announced 36,000 houses for police personnel under the “Your Own Home” scheme.

On 7 May 2012 she announced a ₹1,500-crore scheme to store floodwaters in the Cauvery Delta; on 9 May 2012, a ₹1,420-crore scheme to connect Mamallapuram and Ennore Port. She could have explained what happened to all these projects announced in the Assembly under Rule 110. Instead, she cited very ordinary announcements—upgrading schools, increasing compensation for deaths caused by wild animals, and constructing storage godowns—as schemes she had implemented.

Two years in office are now complete. What is the situation? Prices continue to rise sky-high. Even vegetable prices are beyond control. The state of law and order need hardly be described. Only yesterday, a person who had come to give evidence at the Egmore court was repeatedly hacked; he survived by running into the judge's chamber. A patient undergoing treatment at Chennai General Hospital was killed there. Under this government, farmers, traders, workers—every section has been affected.

These two years have seen unprecedented power cuts: fifteen hours in villages. Factories in Coimbatore, Tiruppur, Erode and Karur districts lie closed, and workers are travelling to other States in search of employment. In the Cauvery Delta districts, farmers could not even cultivate last year.

And in this condition, the government has issued four-page advertisements in English and Tamil newspapers proclaiming “two years of achievement”, attempting thereby to place a lock on those newspapers' mouths. There is no democracy in the Assembly. No member is given an opportunity to speak against the government. Even outside the Assembly, if anyone speaks against the government, defamation cases immediately follow. Newspapers too do not escape defamation cases.

No minister has any authority. Even announcements worth a mere ₹1 crore are made by the Chief Minister herself—not during debate, but under Rule 110, when no one can rise to question them. Immediately, speeches of praise follow. This is what is happening. As for vindictiveness, there is no need even to ask.

If a scheme was implemented by the previous government, it is shelved. Examples include the Sethu Samudram project and the Maduravoyal–Ennore Port link-road project. The State Government that ought to urge the Union Government to complete such projects has gone to the Supreme Court to say that one of those projects is not wanted. Overall, the absolute truth is that this government is being swept along in a rain of praise and a flood of advertisements.
With affection, M.K. 18 May 2013
